sections.h2: What makes Ohio different for a home seller?
sections.html:
Ohio writes its property, probate, foreclosure and tenant rules at the state level, then leaves their daily handling to county offices. The state joined the Union on March 1, 1803. Columbus is both the capital and the largest city, and Cleveland, Cincinnati and Columbus anchor its biggest metro areas. The Census Bureau counts 40,858.76 square miles of land and estimates 11,900,510 people for mid-2025.

A seller in Toledo, Dayton, Akron or a small township works under one Revised Code but meets a different auditor, recorder, treasurer, probate court and clerk of courts in each county. This site follows that split. Statewide pages explain the law, and the city and county pages explain the offices.

sections.h2: What does Ohio's land and housing mix mean for a sale?
sections.html:
Population density was 288.8 per square mile in 2020, and the state mixes dense blocks in Cleveland and Columbus with farm townships. Commutes average 23.4 minutes for workers aged 16 and over, which shapes how far buyers will search from a job center. Monthly owner costs have a midpoint of $1,517 with a mortgage and $588 without one, a range that frames what a buyer can carry.

Sellers whose homes need work often weigh a cash sale against the delay and cost of repairs before listing.

  • Dense counties tend to have more recorded sales to support a valuation complaint.
  • Rural counties may have few comparable sales, so a tax appeal can rest on the house's condition.
  • Cities add permits and codes on top of state law, so check city hall as well as the county.

sections.h2: What does Ohio's economy mean for demand on the housing market?
sections.html:
Buyer demand follows jobs. The Census Bureau counts 255,049 employer establishments in the state for 2023, with total employment of 5,081,279, a gain of 2.4 percent over 2022. Across Ohio, 63.0 percent of residents aged 16 and over were in the civilian labor force for 2020 to 2024, and 31.5 percent of adults aged 25 and over held a bachelor's degree or higher.

Those totals say little about any one street, but they show a state with a deep base of employers. A seller in a county that gained jobs may see more local interest than one in a county where large employers have cut back. The county pages are the place to look for that detail, and a local agent or appraiser can speak to the street itself.

sections.h2: How do Ohio property tax appeals and transfer charges work?
sections.html:
Valuation disputes begin at the county auditor. R.C. 5715.19 sets a March 31 filing date for the following tax year, or the close of first-half collection when that comes later, and the county board of revision hears the case. A repeat complaint on the same parcel waits until a new interim period unless a sale between unrelated parties, a casualty loss, a substantial improvement or a swing of at least fifteen percent in occupancy intervenes.

At closing, a county can levy a transfer tax of no more than thirty cents per hundred dollars of value under R.C. 322.02. The seller named in the deed pays the auditor before recording. Counties set their own rates, so the county guide for the property carries the number.

sections.h2: How do probate, transfer on death affidavits and foreclosure sales work in Ohio?
sections.html:
An estate goes through the probate court that serves the decedent's home county. That court can release a small estate from administration, with limits of $35,000 or $100,000 depending on who inherits (R.C. 2113.03), and executors sell land under R.C. 2127.01 through 2127.43. Ohio no longer taxes estates for deaths from 2013 forward, and the Department of Taxation says the 2021 sunset ended collection on older ones.

An owner can also record a transfer on death affidavit with the county recorder so that title passes to named beneficiaries at death (R.C. 5302.22).

Foreclosure runs through the courts. R.C. 2323.07 says a foreclosed mortgage leads to a sale ordered by the court, which may direct the officer to sell parcels separately or the whole tract and may assign the sheriff or master in each county where the land lies. Anyone hoping to stop a sale has to move before the court enters that order.

sections.h2: How do tenant rules affect selling a rented Ohio house?
sections.html:
A tenant in the house adds a notice calendar and a court calendar. Landlords give at least three days of written notice before filing (R.C. 1923.04), thirty days before the next periodic rental date to end a month-to-month tenancy (R.C. 5321.17), and the first hearing falls no sooner than the seventh day after service. Lockouts and utility shutoffs are barred (R.C. 5321.15).

  • The eviction notice page sets out each notice type.
  • The eviction process page walks through summons, hearing and writ.
  • Read both pages before you commit to a closing date on a rented house.

sections.h2: Which county office handles which step in Ohio?
sections.html:
Property work is spread across several county offices, so one statewide rule can feel different from county to county.

  • Auditor: valuation complaints and the transfer tax paid at deed delivery.
  • Recorder: deeds, transfer on death affidavits and recorded liens.
  • Treasurer: tax bills and payments.
  • Probate court: estates, releases from administration and land sales by fiduciaries.
  • Municipal or county court clerk: eviction filings and summons service.
  • Sheriff: writs and sales ordered in foreclosure cases.

Ask each office for its current forms and fees, which change more often than statutes do. Phone hours and counter locations differ by county, so confirm them with the office before you drive over with a deed or a complaint.

sections.h2: How should I use the Ohio guides on this site?
sections.html: Pick the statewide topic page that matches the problem, whether probate, foreclosure, eviction or estate tax, and then open the county or city guide for the house itself. The county recorder guides cover deed recording, the property tax guides cover the auditor and treasurer, and city pages cover local selling conditions. A problem that spans topics, such as an inherited rental with a tenant, calls for the probate and eviction pages together.

faqs.q: What is the latest population estimate for Ohio?
faqs.a: About 11.9 million. The Census Bureau lists 11,900,510 for mid-2025, up 0.9 percent from its April 2020 estimates base.

faqs.q: How many Ohio homes have the owner living in them?
faqs.a: Roughly two thirds: the Census Bureau gives 67.2 percent, with a midpoint value of $214,800 for those homes.

faqs.q: Where is a valuation complaint filed in Ohio?
faqs.a: With the county auditor, by March 31 of the following tax year or the close of first-half collection if that is later. The county board of revision then hears it, under R.C. 5715.19.

faqs.q: Is there a transfer tax on an Ohio home sale?
faqs.a: Counties may charge one. Under R.C. 322.02 a county can levy no more than thirty cents for each hundred dollars of value, and the seller settles it with the auditor ahead of recording. The auditor can quote the local rate.

faqs.q: Does Ohio still have an estate tax?
faqs.a: No. The Department of Taxation says the estate tax was repealed for deaths in 2013 and later, and that no tax is due on property first discovered after December 31, 2021.
